property_summary: For any caller who is the current owner and any provided newOwner address, after transferOwnership(newOwner) completes the contract's owner() equals the provided newOwner; the mutant instead sets owner() to msg.sender for some inputs, violating this rule.

For any caller who is the current owner and any provided newOwner (which may be any address, including the zero address), calling transferOwnership(newOwner) results in owner() equaling the provided newOwner; the mutant instead sets owner() to msg.sender for some inputs and thus can violate this equality.

For any current owner caller and any provided newOwner address, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner becomes equal to the provided newOwner; the mutant instead sometimes sets owner to msg.sender, breaking this equality.

For any caller who is the current owner and any provided newOwner that is different from the caller, after transferOwnership(newOwner) completes the contract's owner() equals the provided newOwner (the mutant incorrectly sets owner to msg.sender, so when newOwner != msg.sender it will break this).

For any caller who is the current owner and any provided newOwner (non-zero, possibly equal to caller), after transferOwnership(newOwner) completes the contract's owner() equals the provided newOwner; the mutant that assigns msg.sender instead will violate this when newOwner != msg.sender (so we require the caller to be the current owner and newOwner != address(0)).

For every caller address newOwner, when the current owner calls transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's public owner must become newOwner; the mutant that deletes the assignment can be called successfully but leaves owner unchanged, violating this rule for some fuzzed newOwner values.

For any address newOwner, when the current owner calls transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's public owner getter must equal newOwner afterwards; the mutant that omits the assignment call leaves owner unchanged for some fuzzed newOwner values and thus violates this property.

For any address newOwner (fuzzed), if the current owner calls transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's public owner getter must equal newOwner afterwards; the mutant that deletes the assignment leaves owner unchanged for some newOwner inputs, so this assertion will fail on the mutant.

For any address newOwner and when the current owner calls transferOwnership(newOwner), the contract's public owner getter returns newOwner afterwards; the mutant that deletes the assignment leaves owner unchanged for some newOwner inputs and thus violates this rule.

For any nonzero address newOwner, when the current owner calls transferOwnership(newOwner), the contract's public owner getter becomes newOwner; the mutant that removes the assignment leaves owner unchanged for some newOwner values (breaking this rule).

For any nonzero newOwner address provided by the current owner, transferOwnership always updates C.owner to that address; the mutant (which rejects zero addresses) can block ownership changes by reverting when newOwner==address(0), violating the universal property that owner becomes the supplied newOwner for all inputs (including zero).

For any caller who is the current owner and any proposed newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) succeeds and sets owner() to newOwner; the mutant that forbids address(0) breaks this rule because it reverts when newOwner == address(0).

For any caller who is the current owner and any proposed newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) completes (does not revert) and sets owner() == newOwner; the mutant that rejects address(0) violates this because calls with newOwner == address(0) revert and so owner() is not updated.

For any caller who is the current owner and any proposed newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) does not revert and after the call owner() equals newOwner; the mutant that inserts require(newOwner != address(0)) can make calls with newOwner == address(0) revert, violating this property.

For any caller who is the current owner and any non-zero proposed newOwner, transferOwnership(newOwner) completes and sets owner() == newOwner; the mutant that requires newOwner != address(0) still satisfies this for non-zero newOwner but would revert on zero, so we restrict fuzzing to allow only non-zero newOwner to make the property universal for the reference and still detect attempts to set zero if allowed (the test ensures only non-zero are admissible).

Invariant: calling transferOwnership(newOwner) by the current owner always updates C.owner() to newOwner; the mutant inverts the ownership check so a call by the current owner will be rejected and thus owner will not be updated for some inputs.

For any caller address a and any newOwner address n, calling transferOwnership(n) succeeds when msg.sender == owner and updates owner to n; the mutant that restricts onlyOwner to address(0) prevents non-zero owners from successfully calling transferOwnership, so for some fuzzed owner/caller values the reference updates owner but the mutant does not.

For any caller address msgSender and any newOwner, if msgSender is the current owner then transferOwnership(newOwner) succeeds and c.owner() equals newOwner afterwards; the mutant blocks all non-zero senders (only allows address(0)) so there exist owner/caller inputs where the reference updates owner but the mutant does not.

For any caller address caller and any newOwner address newOwner, if caller equals the current owner then calling transferOwnership(newOwner) succeeds (does not revert) and afterwards c.owner() == newOwner; the mutant requiring msg.sender == address(0) will cause such a call to revert (or fail to update owner) for some caller/owner combinations where caller == owner != address(0).
Rule: calling owned() by the current owner must NOT change the owner state (owner remains the same); the mutant assigns owner = address(0) inside owned(), violating this for calls made by the owner.

For any caller who is the contract owner, calling owned() does not change the owner state: after owned() returns the owner getter still equals the original owner; the mutant that assigns owner = address(0) inside owned() violates this for owner callers.

For any address caller that is the current owner, invoking owned() must preserve the owner state (owner remains equal to the caller); the mutant that assigns owner = address(0) inside owned() breaks this by changing owner to zero for some owner caller.

For every caller who is not the current owner, calling owned() must revert (onlyOwner modifier); the mutant that assigns owner = address(0) inside owned() still preserves the modifier but onlyOwner ensures non-owners cannot call — thus the reference always reverts for non-owners while the mutant may still revert; to distinguish, we instead assert that when the owner calls owned(), the owner remains equal to the original owner after the call (the reference preserves owner, the mutant sets owner to address(0) and thus breaks this).

For any address set as owner via transferOwnership, calling owned() (by that owner) must not change the owner stored in the contract; the mutant that assigns owner = address(0) inside owned() violates this by setting owner to zero for some owner callers.

The owner-only modifier guarantees that calling owned() cannot change the owner: for every caller address, after calling owned() the owner() getter remains equal to the pre-call owner; the mutant removing the require allows non-owners to call owned() and therefore may change owner for some caller addresses.

For every caller address, calling owned() does not change the contract's owner (owner() remains equal to its pre-call value); the mutant removes the onlyOwner check so some caller can change owner via owned() and thus violate this invariance.

For every caller address, calling owned() must NOT modify the public owner() value (owner stays equal to pre-call owner); the mutant removes the onlyOwner check so a malicious caller contract can call owned() and mutate owner, violating this property for some inputs.
For any caller address, only the current owner can change C.owner via transferOwnership; the mutant that removes the onlyOwner guard allows some non-owner caller to change owner.
